summary: Asked, for the first time, whether the WIRE under mypintusan's decisions survives what actually happens to an RS-485 segment in a building (tools/fleetbench/bench_pintusan_bus.py, 42 checks over 10 episodes; item 5 of the hardening register for the app that physically opens doors, after Secure Channel, the six alarms, offline mode and schedules). It drives the rest of the fault table in docs/MYPINTUSAN_OSDP_PLAN.md 4.1 - busy, bad-sequence, bad-crc, garbage, one-down, slow, addr-collision - and it is the first exercise of the reconnect path at all. WHY IT TAKES A LIVE APPLIANCE: bus_test.go is 733 lines and good, and every one of its cases runs over an in-memory net.Pipe that is never torn down mid-run, so the chain from failPort through Run returning, superviseBus re-dialling, a fresh Bus and Controller being built and the site's lockdown being carried into them has no coverage at that layer and cannot have one. Killing a simulator is the only way to ask, and that takes a real process to kill. FOUR DEFECTS. (1) THE FAULT WITH THE BIGGEST BLAST RADIUS WAS THE ONLY SILENT ONE. A reader that stops answering is alarmed, because Run keeps polling and each timeout counts against OfflineAfter. A dead PORT is not: failPort ends the run on the very next slot - deliberately, so the owner can re-dial - which is long before any reader has failed the three transactions that declare it offline. So unplugging the adapter took every door on the segment out of service, raised NO alarm of any kind, and left every reader row reading 'ok, last seen a moment ago'. Measured live: forty-five seconds after the cable came out, the alarm feed held NOTHING AT ALL - not one notification of any category. New services.Controller.BusDown marks every reader on the segment offline - without moving LastSeenAt, which belongs to when the reader last ANSWERED, not to when we gave up on it - and raises one new AlarmBusOffline ('OSDP segment down - every door on it is out of service') naming the port and the reader count. One alarm for the cable rather than one per reader, because eight pages for one cable is how people learn to dismiss alarms - and one alarm per OUTAGE rather than per failed re-dial, since a gateway that is rebooting accepts the connection and drops it again for as long as that takes, and paging on each of those would deliver the alarm-fatigue failure alarm.go argues against through the very alarm added to prevent silence; a session lasting 20s ends the outage and re-arms it, the same threshold that resets the backoff in (3). Both halves matter: marking the rows is what stops the screen lying to the person the alarm just woke. (2) EVERY PROTOCOL FAULT REACHED THE OPERATOR AS 'READER SECURE CHANNEL FAULT'. osdp.EventFault covers a skewed sequence number, a NAKed command, an undecodable PDID, a card read that will not parse AND a failed Secure Channel handshake, and the controller mapped the whole kind to AlarmSecureChannel. Measured against the bad-sequence scenario, on a reader with no Secure Channel configured at all: headline 'Reader secure channel fault', body 'reply sequence 1, expected 0 - resetting the session'. That is the right alarm under a headline that sends an installer hunting for a bus tap while the actual fault is cabling or firmware. Fixed with Event.Fault (FaultProtocol / FaultSecureChannel; the zero value is FaultProtocol so an unclassified fault errs towards 'wiring' rather than 'security', because over-reporting security faults is how an operator learns to ignore them), set at the three secure-channel emission sites in bus.go, and a new AlarmBusFault - 'Reader communication fault - check the wiring'. This was recorded as an unproven lead by the alarms bench and is now settled. (3) THE RE-DIAL BACKOFF NEVER RESET, SO EVERY RECOVERY MADE THE NEXT ONE SLOWER, PERMANENTLY. superviseBus's 1s-to-30s backoff exists so an absent adapter does not spin, and is capped so that 'a door that comes back must not wait minutes to be polled again'. It doubled on every attempt and was never returned to its floor, so it accumulated over the life of the PROCESS rather than over the current outage: a site whose gateway reboots nightly, or whose cable is knocked by a cleaner once a week, reached the cap after about five events and stayed there. Measured live: after four knocks and thirty seconds of perfectly healthy running the sixth reconnect took 28.5s, against 5.2s for the same knock on the fixed build - so every door on the segment stayed dead for half a minute after the cable was already back, which is the exact delay the cap exists to prevent. Fixed: a session that ran for 20s or more resets the backoff to its floor, because a session that RAN is the end of an outage, not a step deeper into one. (4) A SEGMENT THAT CANNOT ENROL A READER LEAKED ITS CONNECTION ON EVERY RE-DIAL. runBus dials first and enrols second, and Bus closes the port in Run's defer and nowhere else - so the 'no usable readers' path returned without closing anything while superviseBus retried for ever. One requireSecureChannel with no key, or one mistyped 16-byte SCBK, on a single-reader segment is enough to take that path, and both are refused per-reader on purpose (a mistyped key must never silently become a cleartext session). Measured: 10 established connections after 75s of re-dialling against a simulator with no reader being polled, where the fixed build holds none - and bounded only by Go's finalizer eventually closing sockets the process no longer references, which is a garbage-collection schedule and not a resource policy. It matters more than an ordinary leak because the far end is usually a serial-to-Ethernet gateway and those commonly accept one to four TCP clients, so correcting the typo does not necessarily recover the segment: the gateway's client table is full of connections nobody is using and somebody has to go and power-cycle it. Fixed with a defer that closes the transport on every path that does not reach Run. PROVEN GOOD and recorded as such, so it is not re-benched: a sick reader does not take out a healthy one (three readers on one cable, the middle one dies, it is alarmed and its row goes offline while doors 1 and 3 both still open within seconds with their rows still reading ok); nor does a slow one (a reader answering at 800ms against a 1000ms timeout is not declared offline, and the healthy reader beside it grants on a cadence the cable sustains); BUSY is retried rather than treated as death; a reader that is present but unusable does not open a door and is declared offline by the supervision timeout; the three-way awaitReply diagnosis reaches the operator VERBATIM and is the most valuable thing in this area (bad-crc produces 'frame(s) arrived but failed CRC - check 120 ohm termination at both ends, shield grounded at one end only, and cable length', addr-collision produces 'bytes received but no frame decoded - likely two readers sharing address 0, or a badly terminated segment'); the appliance keeps serving through corrupted CRCs, junk with stray SOMs and two PDs fighting over address 0; and LOCKDOWN SURVIVES AN UNPLUGGED ADAPTER END TO END - sealed, badge denied lockdown, cable pulled, the API still reporting the site sealed while the segment is down, cable back, a badge on the RECONNECTED bus still denied lockdown, then lifted and the same badge granted. REPORTED, NOT BUILT: Bus.Stats() returns a full PDStats per reader (transactions, timeouts, CRC errors, NAKs, BUSY replies, sequence errors, offline transitions, secure-channel failures, unframed bytes) and its own comment says why they matter - 'a bus with failing termination or a ground loop shows a rising CrcErrors long before any reader actually drops offline' - and nothing outside a test calls it; nor does anything call Bus.Dropped(), the count of events discarded because the consumer stalled, which is to say badges that never reached a decision. No API field, no endpoint, no screen. TOOLING: five more simulator scenarios could not demonstrate their own claim because they presented no card at all - busy, bad-sequence, bad-crc, garbage and addr-collision are each a claim about a DOOR, and none of them could offer a credential. All five now run a cardLoop, which is what lets this bench say 'no door opens on a cable whose frames cannot be trusted' rather than 'no frame was decoded'; addr-collision badges at address 0 from BOTH colliding PDs, which is the out-of-box case as an installer meets it. pintusan_harness.boot() gained readers= (a multi-PD segment - one-down, multidrop and slow are unaskable on a one-reader bus) plus slot_millis / reply_timeout_millis / status_millis. 42/42 checks pass with the fixes; 36/42 against the unfixed app.
compatibility: Backward-compatible; no schema change, no config change, no API surface change. Two new alarm KINDS appear in the notification feed under existing machinery: access.bus-fault ('Reader communication fault - check the wiring') and access.bus-offline ('OSDP segment down - every door on it is out of service'), both WARNING like every non-duress, non-forced alarm. An operator will notice two changes, both of them the point of the work. First, protocol faults that used to arrive titled 'Reader secure channel fault' now arrive under the communication headline instead; anything filtering or alerting on the access.secure-channel category will see fewer of them, and what remains is genuinely about the encrypted session. Second, an OSDP segment losing its transport now raises an alarm where it previously raised none, and marks every reader on that segment offline in the readers list - a site with a genuinely flaky adapter will start seeing an alarm per outage that it never saw before, which is the correct report of a condition that was always happening. osdp.Event gained a Fault field (zero value FaultProtocol, so an unset one is reported as a wiring fault, the safe direction); infra/access/osdp has exactly one consumer today, and a future second one that ignores the field simply gets the old undifferentiated behaviour. The re-dial backoff now returns to 1s after a bus session that ran 20s or more, so a segment that has recovered before comes back as fast as one that never failed; nothing waits longer than it used to. Scope is `infra` rather than `mypintusan`: mypintusan has no entry in infra/versioning/version.json's apps map yet, and an unknown scope token hard-fails the release run.
